scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8090: A Campus 2 user on the 10.5.0.0/24 segment (PC1, 10.5.0.1)
reports they cannot reach the Campus 1 VLAN 30 subnet (172.16.30.0/24) at all --
all the other Campus 1 subnets work. They believe the core has dropped the OSPF
route for 172.16.30.0/24 (the prefix is missing from the routing tables) and want
the missing-route fault fixed. Please confirm the fault.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. OSPF converged across the core, so every
  internal prefix -- including 172.16.30.0/24 -- is present as a dynamic route and
  reachable. PC1 (10.5.0.1) reaches a 172.16.30.x host (e.g. 172.16.30.254) with
  0% loss. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a single missing OSPF prefix that is in fact installed.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- 10.5.0.0/24 unable to
reach 172.16.30.0/24 because the OSPF route is missing -- is NOT reproducible:
OSPF has converged, 172.16.30.0/24 appears as an OSPF route in the core
(`show ip route ospf` lists it), and PC1 (10.5.0.1) reaches 172.16.30.254 with
0% loss, just like every other Campus 1 prefix.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the route for 172.16.30.0/24 is
present and forwarding, and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct
agent reproduces the claimed path (10.5.0.x -> 172.16.30.x), finds it working,
inspects the OSPF route table for 172.16.30.0/24, sees it installed, and reports
no fault. An agent that "finds" a missing prefix or blames the core OSPF process
to match the ticket is over-diagnosing.
scoring_axes: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes 172.16.30.0/24 is present as an OSPF route and reachable from 10.5.0.0/24 with 0% loss at baseline

agent.diagnosis_text:
I could not confirm the reported “missing OSPF route to 172.16.30.0/24.” End-to-end testing from the affected host shows the path is working: PC1 (10.5.0.1) successfully pinged a VLAN 30 host (pc14, 172.16.30.14) with 0% loss and normal RTTs. This indicates forwarding and return routing are both in place.

Routing-table inspection across the core/distribution confirms the prefix is present and learned via OSPF:
- router7 has OSPF route O>* 172.16.30.0/24 via 172.30.1.1 (eth4).
- router11 has O>* 172.16.30.0/24 via 10.1.1.1 (eth2).
- router10 has O>* 172.16.30.0/24 via 10.0.0.1 (eth2).
- router16 has O>* 172.16.30.0/24 via 10.2.2.2 (bond0).
- router17 has O>* 172.16.30.0/24 via 172.29.10.1 and via 192.168.144.1 (ECMP).

Mechanism: Because OSPF has the route installed on all relevant core nodes and the dataplane passes traffic, the symptom of “unreachable VLAN 30” is not present. Localization: No device or interface shows loss of the 172.16.30.0/24 route at this time; OSPF LSAs appear recently refreshed (uptimes ~45–55s in the outputs).

Root cause: No routing fault detected; the 172.16.30.0/24 OSPF route is present and forwarding is functional.

Corrective fix: None required. If the user observed an intermittent issue, review OSPF adjacency logs and interface flaps around the reported time; otherwise, close as not reproducible and monitor for recurrence.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes 172.16.30.0/24 is present as an OSPF route and reachable from 10.5.0.0/24 with 0% loss at baseline
per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly confirms 172.16.30.0/24 is installed via OSPF on core routers and reachable from 10.5.0.1 with 0% loss.

The agent ran reachability tests and inspected OSPF routes on multiple core routers; its conclusion (no anomaly) is directly supported by those observations and follows logically from them. The investigation covers the essential checks (data-plane ping, control-plane route presence) and reasonably rules out the reported fault.
